- When sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–3% for next period.
- When sentiment is bearish (≤0.33) and prices are trending down, model often underestimates; adjust upward by 1–2% to capture mean reversion.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., +5%+ in 3–5 days), model frequently overshoots in subsequent days; apply a 2–5 day lag correction, dampening forecast slope.
- If sentiment shifts abruptly from bullish to bearish, model often fails to adjust quickly; delay forecast adjustment by 1–2 days and reduce magnitude.
- For 30-day horizon, model tends to overfit recent volatility; apply smoothing filter (e.g., 5-day moving average) to forecast path.
- When sentiment is neutral (0.33–0.67) and history shows no clear trend, model often predicts mean-reversion bias; align forecast to 3–5 day average of recent prices.
- If true outcome is consistently below forecast (e.g., 3–5% gap), model may be overconfident; reduce forecast by 1–2% for next period unless sentiment supports upside.
- If true outcome is consistently above forecast, model may be underestimating sentiment strength; increase forecast by 1–2% if sentiment remains bullish or neutral.
